title: Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) Shares Down 2.3% - Should You Sell? - MarketBeat
content:
Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT - Get Free Report)'s stock price traded down 2.3% on Wednesday . The stock traded as low as $491.52 and last traded at $492.43. 27,286,649 shares changed hands during trading, a decline of 28% from the average daily volume of 37,694,008 shares. The stock had previously closed at $503.81. Here are the key news stories impacting Microsoft this week: Several analysts recently issued reports on the company. Guggenheim  reiterated a "buy" rating and issued a $586.00 price target on shares of Microsoft in a report on Monday, July 27th. UBS Group  set a $525.00 target price on shares of Microsoft in a research report on Thursday, July 30th. Phillip Securities lowered shares of Microsoft from a "strong-buy" rating to a "moderate buy" rating in a report on Monday, August 3rd. China Renaissance cut their price objective on shares of Microsoft from $630.00 to $550.00 and set a "buy" rating on the stock in a report on Monday, May 4th. Finally, Wedbush  reissued an "outperform" rating and issued a $575.00 price objective on shares of Microsoft in a research report on Wednesday, May 13th. Forty-two equities research analysts have rated the stock with a Buy rating and five have assigned  a Hold rating to the stock. According to MarketBeat, Microsoft presently has a consensus rating of "Moderate Buy" and a consensus target price of $560.27. The company has a current ratio of 1.23, a quick ratio of 1.22 and a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.07. The firm has a market capitalization of $3.66 trillion, a price-to-earnings ratio of 27.42, a PEG ratio of 1.63 and a beta of 1.11. The business has a 50-day moving average price of $407.02 and a two-hundred day moving average price of $407.37. Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT - Get Free Report) last announced its quarterly earnings results on Wednesday, July 29th. The software giant reported $4.74 earnings per share (EPS) for the quarter, beating the consensus estimate of $4.24 by $0.50. Microsoft had a net margin of 40.31% and a return on equity of 31.98%. The company had revenue of $90.01 billion during the quarter, compared to the consensus estimate of $87.62 billion. During the same quarter in the previous year, the company posted $3.65 earnings per share. The company's revenue for the quarter was up 17.7% compared to the same quarter last year.  As a group, research analysts forecast that  Microsoft Corporation will post 19.58 EPS for the current year. The company also recently declared a quarterly dividend, which will be paid on Thursday, September 10th. Shareholders of record on Thursday, August 20th will be paid a $0.91 dividend. The ex-dividend date is Thursday, August 20th. This represents a $3.64 annualized dividend and a dividend yield of 0.7%. Microsoft's dividend payout ratio (DPR) is presently 20.27%. In other news, EVP Amy Coleman sold 1,262 shares of the business's stock in a transaction that occurred on Thursday, May 14th. The stock was sold at an average price of $411.34, for a total transaction of $519,111.08. Following the completion of the transaction, the executive vice president directly owned 46,003 shares in the company, valued at approximately $18,922,874.02. The trade was a 2.67% decrease in their ownership of the stock. The sale was disclosed in a filing with the SEC, which is accessible through the SEC website. Also, EVP Takeshi Numoto sold 4,810 shares of the stock in a transaction that occurred on Tuesday, August 4th. The stock was sold at an average price of $496.48, for a total value of $2,388,068.80. Following the completion of the transaction, the executive vice president directly owned 42,677 shares of the company's stock, valued at $21,188,276.96. This trade represents a 10.13% decrease in their ownership of the stock. The SEC filing for this sale provides additional information. Over the last 90 days, insiders have sold 38,572 shares of company stock valued at $17,775,330. Insiders own  0.03% of the company's stock. Large investors have recently modified their holdings of the business. Longfellow Investment Management Co. LLC lifted its position in  Microsoft by 51.3% in the second quarter. Longfellow Investment Management Co. LLC now owns 59 shares of the software giant's stock worth $29,000 after purchasing an additional 20 shares during the period.  Bernzott Capital Advisors acquired a new position in shares of  Microsoft during the 4th quarter valued at $34,000.  Frankly Finances LLC bought a new stake in shares of  Microsoft in the 2nd quarter worth $35,000.  Timmons Wealth Management LLC bought a new stake in shares of  Microsoft in the 4th quarter worth $36,000.  Finally, Bard Associates Inc. acquired a new stake in shares of  Microsoft in the second quarter valued at $37,000. 71.13% of the stock is owned by institutional investors and hedge funds. Microsoft Corporation is a global technology company headquartered in Redmond, Washington. Founded in 1975 by Bill Gates and Paul Allen, Microsoft develops, licenses and supports a broad range of software products, services and devices for consumers, enterprises and governments worldwide. Its operations span personal computing, productivity software, cloud infrastructure, enterprise applications, developer tools and gaming. Microsoft's product portfolio includes the Windows operating system and the Microsoft 365 suite of productivity and collaboration tools (Office apps, Outlook, Teams). title: Applied Digital vs. Microsoft: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? - The Globe and Mail
content: Applied Digital is rapidly expanding its high-performance computing infrastructure. Microsoft leverages a massive ecosystem and strong profitability across diverse segments. Which technology provider is the better fit for your growth strategy? As the race for high-performance computing intensifies, investors must choose between the niche growth of Applied Digital(NASDAQ:APLD) and the massive scale of Microsoft(NASDAQ:MSFT). Which stock is the better buy? Applied Digital builds the physical foundation for the artificial intelligence era through specialized data centers. Microsoft operates as a global technology leader, integrating software and cloud computing across its massive ecosystem. Both companies are prominent players in the technology landscape, though they offer distinct risk and reward profiles for your portfolio. Applied Digital designs and operates digital infrastructure and cloud services for high-performance computing (HPC) and artificial intelligence. The company primarily serves crypto mining customers and provides GPU computing for hyperscalers and enterprises. One anchor customer accounted for roughly 59% of total revenue from continuing operations during fiscal year 2026. Customer concentration like this adds a layer of risk to the business. In FY 2026, revenue reached nearly $611.3 million, marking a significant growth rate of approximately 183.7% compared to the previous year. This expansion was driven by the scaling of its data center and cloud service segments. Despite the revenue surge, the company reported a net loss of nearly $244.0 million for the period. Applied Digital operates within the infrastructure segment of tech stocks. As of its May 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is nearly 2.9x, which shows how much debt a company uses relative to shareholder equity. The current ratio, measuring the ability to cover short term obligations, is approximately 4.0x. Free cash flow was negative at close to $2.8 billion, representing cash from operations minus capital expenditures. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 245.5% of operating cash flow, meaning reported cash generation is heavily inflated by this non-cash add-back. Microsoft develops a wide range of software, cloud services, and hardware for consumers and large global enterprises. Its business spans three major segments including Productivity and Business Processes, Intelligent Cloud, and More Personal Computing. The company maintains a highly diversified customer base and maintains strategic relationships with key entities such as OpenAI. This ecosystem approach allows it to integrate artificial intelligence across a global platform. In FY 2026, revenue reached nearly $331.8 billion, representing a year-over-year increase of approximately 17.8%. The company generated a net income of roughly $133.7 billion, which resulted in a net margin of close to 40.3%. This net margin indicates how much of every dollar in revenue becomes actual profit after all expenses. As of its June 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.3x, showing a low reliance on debt compared to shareholder equity. The current ratio is roughly 1.2x, which reflects the company's ability to pay off short term liabilities with its current assets. Free cash flow was strong at nearly $67 billion, representing the cash generated from operations after subtracting capital expenditures and providing significant flexibility for future growth. Applied Digital faces significant risks related to customer concentration, as a large portion of its revenue comes from a limited number of hyperscale customers. Any deterioration in their financial health could materially impact the business. Operations are heavily concentrated in North Dakota, creating exposure to regional infrastructure and regulatory risks. Furthermore, the company requires substantial capital for data center construction and carries significant debt. Microsoft faces constant cybersecurity threats and data privacy risks that target its internal infrastructure. The company competes in a crowded market for artificial intelligence where Amazon and Alphabet also invest heavily. Global regulatory scrutiny regarding antitrust and AI safety remains an ongoing challenge. Additionally, the company is currently defending against multiple securities fraud class action lawsuits concerning its Copilot AI performance. Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers. I'd go with Microsoft, which just closed an extraordinary fiscal year. To give Applied Digital its due, it is building AI data center infrastructure at a pace that few companies can match, and its most recent quarter was a genuine breakout. Its CoreWeave contract gives it long-term revenue visibility that was not there a year ago. But Applied Digital is still a small, unprofitable business in a capital-intensive industry, and analysts expect earnings to turn sharply negative again over the next year as the company ramps construction. That kind of volatility is a lot to absorb. Microsoft, meanwhile, is reporting record revenue across every major segment. Azure crossed a major milestone for the first time, Copilot paid seats more than doubled in a single quarter, and the company guided for continued acceleration heading into the new fiscal year. The stock had been under pressure for much of 2026 on concerns about AI spending, and the quarter put those concerns to rest in a big way. For a long-term investor, owning one of the most profitable technology companies in the world at a moment when its AI strategy is clearly working is a stronger bet than a data center start-up still finding its financial footing.  stayed near the center of the technology conversation on as traders weighed a sustained wave of spending on artificial intelligence infrastructure against a jittery mood in semiconductor names. The company, which sits at the intersection of cloud computing, enterprise software, and machine learning tools, has come to represent much of what the broad market associates with the current buildout of computing capacity. As Wall Street traded cautiously ahead of fresh inflation data, the software giant offered a reminder that the technology story runs deeper than any single chip supplier. The technology sector has spent recent sessions caught between two opposing forces. On one side stands an enormous, ongoing commitment by the largest cloud operators to expand data-center capacity, acquire advanced processors, and build out the physical foundation for artificial intelligence workloads. On the other side sits a wave of caution about how that spending is financed, whether demand can keep pace with supply, and how competition from abroad might reshape the landscape. Microsoft occupies a distinctive position in this debate because it both procures vast computing resources and provides the software and cloud services that run on top of them. Semiconductor names saw a sharp selloff during the week, driven in part by unease about circular-financing arrangements, in which suppliers, customers, and partners are tied together through overlapping commitments, and by renewed concern about competition from Chinese chipmakers. That pullback rattled sentiment across the wider group. Yet the software and cloud layer of the sector has shown more resilience, in part because recurring subscription revenue and enterprise contracts tend to be less exposed to the day-to-day swings in hardware pricing. Microsoft operates across several large and interlocking segments. Its productivity and business-process division includes the widely used suite of office applications, collaboration tools, and the professional networking platform that connects working people around the world. Its intelligent-cloud division houses the Azure platform, which provides computing power, storage, databases, and a growing catalog of artificial intelligence services to organizations of every size. A third area brings together the Windows operating system, gaming through its console and subscription offerings, devices, and advertising. This breadth means the company is not dependent on any single product cycle. When one area faces headwinds, another can provide balance. The cloud division has drawn the most attention lately because it serves as the delivery mechanism for many of the artificial intelligence capabilities that enterprises are eager to adopt. Businesses that want to embed machine learning into their own applications frequently turn to large cloud platforms rather than build the underlying infrastructure themselves, and Microsoft has positioned Azure to capture that demand. The defining industry development of the moment is the scale of capital being committed to computing infrastructure. Hyperscale operators  the handful of companies that run the largest cloud platforms  have signaled that spending on servers, networking gear, and specialized processors will remain elevated. This commitment underpins demand for advanced chips and for the electrical and cooling systems that data centers require. Microsoft is among the operators driving that spending, building and leasing capacity to meet what it describes as strong appetite for artificial intelligence services. At the same time, the market has grown more discerning about how this buildout is being funded and whether the rewards will justify the outlays. Reports of intertwined financing among chipmakers, cloud providers, and artificial intelligence developers prompted questions about whether demand signals are as independent as they appear. Microsoft, with its large and diversified base of enterprise customers, is often cited as one of the operators whose commitments rest on genuine, recurring business rather than on speculative arrangements. That distinction has helped the software layer stand up better than the pure-hardware names during bouts of caution. The broader market environment on was defined by patience. Traders across the Nasdaq Composite and other benchmarks appeared reluctant to make large commitments ahead of fresh inflation data that could shape expectations for monetary conditions. Technology names, which tend to be sensitive to shifts in the cost of money, were especially exposed to that hesitation. Cooler price pressures generally ease conditions for long-duration growth companies, while hotter readings can weigh on them. Within this backdrop, the sharp selloff in chip names created cross-currents. Some traders treated the pullback as a reason to step back from the entire technology complex, while others drew a line between hardware suppliers and the software and services companies that sit above them. Microsoft, as a diversified operator with deep enterprise relationships, tended to be grouped with the latter. A premarket rebound in one of the most closely watched chip designers also helped steady the mood, reminding the market that sentiment in the group can shift quickly. Microsoft's positioning rests on the durability of its enterprise relationships and the breadth of its offerings. Large organizations frequently standardize on its productivity software, its identity and security tools, and its cloud platform, creating a web of commitments that tends to persist across economic cycles. This installed base gives the company a channel through which to distribute new artificial intelligence features, since customers already using its tools can adopt additional capabilities without switching providers. The company has woven machine learning assistants into many of its products, from writing and spreadsheet tools to software-development environments and customer-service applications. This approach aims to make artificial intelligence a routine part of everyday work rather than a separate, specialized add-on. By embedding these features across a familiar suite, Microsoft seeks to convert broad usage into deeper engagement, which in turn supports demand for the cloud capacity that powers those features. Several trends are shaping the technology sector as the buildout continues. The first is the shift of computing workloads toward specialized processors designed for machine learning, which has reordered the supply chain and concentrated attention on a small number of advanced chip designers and manufacturers. The second is the growing importance of electrical power and cooling, as data centers consume enormous amounts of energy and operators race to secure reliable supply. The third is the migration of enterprise software toward subscription and cloud-delivered models, which smooths revenue and ties customers more closely to their providers. Microsoft is exposed to each of these trends. It is a major purchaser of specialized processors, a large builder of energy-intensive data centers, and one of the pioneers of the subscription software model. This alignment means the company's fortunes are closely tied to the pace and health of the broader buildout, even as its diversified structure gives it some insulation from the swings that hit narrower hardware names. Recent developments across the group have underscored how sentiment can turn on questions of financing and competition rather than on the underlying demand for computing. The selloff in chip names was driven less by weak orders than by unease about the structure of the market and by the prospect of stronger competition from abroad. For a diversified operator like Microsoft, these concerns are more indirect. Its cloud platform depends on a steady supply of advanced hardware, so anything that disrupts chip availability or pricing matters, but its revenue does not rise and fall with the price of individual processors. The premarket steadying in one prominent chip designer offered a counterpoint to the week's caution, and it reinforced a pattern that has recurred throughout the buildout: sharp pullbacks followed by attempts at stabilization as traders reassess the long-run demand picture. Microsoft, sitting above the hardware layer, tends to experience these episodes as ripples rather than as direct shocks. The sector faces real challenges even amid the enthusiasm. Building and operating data centers at scale requires vast capital, reliable energy, and skilled personnel, and the payoff depends on sustained demand for artificial intelligence services. If adoption slows or if the economics of these services disappoint, the heavy spending now under way could weigh on the operators who committed to it. Competition is intensifying as well, both among the cloud platforms themselves and from chipmakers abroad who are working to close the gap with established suppliers. Microsoft must also manage the complexity of serving enterprise customers who are increasingly attentive to data security, privacy, and the reliability of the tools they depend on. As artificial intelligence features spread through its products, the company faces scrutiny over how those features handle sensitive information and how accurately they perform. Meeting these expectations is essential to sustaining the trust that underpins its enterprise relationships. The competitive landscape in cloud and enterprise software remains intense. A small number of large platforms compete for the same enterprise workloads, each racing to offer the most capable and cost-effective artificial intelligence services. Microsoft competes against other major cloud operators, against specialized software firms, and against the chance that large customers will build their own capabilities in-house. Its answer has been to combine scale, a broad product suite, and deep integration across the tools that businesses already use. In the artificial intelligence arena specifically, the company has aligned itself with leading model developers while also building its own capabilities, seeking to offer customers a range of options. This dual approach reflects the uncertainty of a fast-moving field in which today's leading model can be surpassed quickly. By keeping its platform open to multiple approaches, Microsoft aims to remain relevant regardless of which techniques ultimately prevail. Much of Microsoft's operational attention now centers on scaling data-center capacity in a disciplined way. Building these facilities involves securing land, arranging reliable electrical supply, installing cooling systems capable of handling dense racks of specialized processors, and coordinating a global network so that services respond quickly wherever customers are located. Each of these steps carries its own constraints, from the availability of power in a given region to the lead times for critical equipment. The company has described an approach that balances aggressive expansion with attention to how quickly newly built capacity is put to work, since idle infrastructure represents cost without matching demand. Software delivery is the other half of the operational picture. Rolling out artificial intelligence features across a suite used by an enormous base of organizations requires careful engineering to keep those tools reliable, secure, and consistent. Updates must be tested against countless configurations, and new capabilities must be introduced without disrupting the workflows that businesses depend on every day. This operational discipline is less visible than the construction of data centers, but it is equally important to sustaining the trust that keeps enterprise customers engaged. The interplay between physical infrastructure and software refinement defines how the company translates ambition into services that function at scale. The scale of spending across the cloud group has drawn attention to how operators manage the tension between building ahead of demand and avoiding overextension. Committing capital to data centers years before the associated services are fully utilized requires confidence that demand will materialize, and it exposes operators to the possibility that appetite could soften. Microsoft has framed its spending as a response to concrete demand signals from enterprise customers rather than as speculative construction, a distinction the market has treated as meaningful during recent bouts of caution around the sector. Discipline in this context means aligning the pace of construction with the rhythm of adoption, so that capacity comes online roughly when it is needed rather than long before or after. It also means designing facilities that can adapt as processor technology evolves, since the hardware installed today be superseded by more capable chips within a relatively short span. Operators that manage this balance well can support growing demand without straining their finances, while those that misjudge it can find themselves carrying costly infrastructure that outpaces usage. For a company of Microsoft's scale, these choices reverberate across the broader sector, because its commitments help set the tone for how the entire cloud group approaches the buildout. Microsoft's broad footprint gives it outsized relevance to the wider market. Because it sits within the most heavily weighted corners of major benchmarks, its movements can influence the direction of major technology benchmarks and other indices. Traders often treat the company as a barometer for the health of enterprise technology spending and for the durability of the artificial intelligence buildout. When sentiment toward the sector shifts, Microsoft frequently moves with it, and its scale means those moves ripple across funds and portfolios that track the broad market. This relevance also means the company draws intense scrutiny during periods of caution like the present one. As traders await inflation data and weigh the questions swirling around chip financing and foreign competition, Microsoft's diversified structure and recurring revenue make it a reference point for how the market is thinking about the endurance of the technology theme. Its ability to keep converting cloud and software demand into steady business is central to the broader narrative around US technology names. title: Palantir (NASDAQ: PLTR) Posts 93% Revenue Jump But Faces Steep Valuation Hurdle Against Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Comeback - foreignpolicyjournal.com
content: By Ewan Scott | Aug 12, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ: PLTR) surged as much as 14% in after-hours trading following a strong quarterly earnings report released on August 3, 2026. The gains came after a brutal nine-month slide that erased more than 40% of the stock’s value from its November peak. Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ: MSFT) recently delivered one of the most dramatic earnings rallies in its history, rising roughly 25% across three trading days. That run included a record single-day market cap gain of $450 billion, setting a high bar that Palantir investors are now hoping their company can match. Ahead of Palantir’s earnings report, options traders purchased twice as many call options as put options, anticipating a price swing of over 10%. That bet paid off decisively, as Palantir’s revenue jumped 93% to $1.94 billion, surpassing analyst expectations of $1.80 billion. Adjusted earnings came in at 41 cents per share, beating the 35 cents analysts had forecast, while the company raised its full-year revenue outlook to as much as $8.16 billion. CEO Alex Karp described commercial demand as “otherworldly,” and told shareholders the business is “compounding at a rate and scale that we have never before witnessed.” U.S. government revenue climbed 90% to $809 million, underscoring Palantir’s deepening ties with federal defense and intelligence clients. Microsoft’s own recovery was driven by investor conviction that its heavy AI capital spending is beginning to generate real returns, with options strategist Mike Khouw noting the stock’s “immediate binary event risk is officially behind us.” At roughly 22.6 times forward earnings, Microsoft now trades near the midpoint of its 20-year valuation range, a relatively modest multiple given its mid-teens revenue growth trajectory. Palantir, by contrast, trades at approximately 67 times forward earnings, making it one of the most expensive stocks in the S&P 500 and the single most expensive by price-to-sales ratio. That elevated valuation means one strong quarter may not be sufficient to fully reverse a bear market that has already wiped out more than 40% of investor value. The company also faces operational headwinds, including France’s domestic intelligence agency dropping Palantir in favor of French rival ChapsVision, and an ongoing legal dispute over a blocked London police contract. Of the 33 analysts currently tracking the stock, 22 rate it a “Buy,” reflecting cautious but meaningful confidence in the company’s growth trajectory. Hedge fund interest tells a similar story, with Insider Monkey’s database showing Palantir held by 96 hedge funds as of Q1 2026, up from 89 the prior quarter, while Microsoft attracted 282 holders despite a decline from 312. Among enterprise software peers tracked by Insider Monkey, Oracle had 115 hedge fund holders, ServiceNow had 108, and Snowflake had 80, all trailing Microsoft’s institutional support by a wide margin. The comparison between the two companies highlights a broader market question about whether explosive growth metrics can justify premium valuations when a stock has already suffered a prolonged drawdown. Microsoft’s recovery demonstrated that a credible earnings catalyst can reignite institutional confidence quickly, but Palantir’s far steeper multiple means the market will demand sustained proof before declaring its own bear market over.  attracted steady attention on Wednesday as US equity indices lingered near record highs in a cautious pause ahead of the July Consumer Price Index report due the following day. Trading across the broad market carried the muted, wait-and-see quality typical of late summer, with thin volumes and climbing Treasury yields shaping how names across the technology complex moved through the session. Against that backdrop, the software and cloud giant remained one of the most closely watched members of the large-capitalization group, its scale and reach making it a natural reference point whenever the market pauses to reassess conditions. For more coverage, see Bluechip Stocks. The mood across trading desks reflected a market that had climbed to elevated levels and was now waiting for confirmation from incoming economic data before committing to a fresh direction. Inflation readings have taken on outsized importance in recent months, and the approaching print gave the broad tape a reason to tread carefully. Within that environment, the largest technology names tended to trade in a measured fashion, and Microsoft was no exception, moving quietly as the market collectively held its breath for the numbers ahead. The term bluechip describes large, well-established companies with long operating histories, broad recognition, and business models that have weathered multiple economic cycles. These are the names that anchor major indices and often set the tone for the wider market. Microsoft sits comfortably within this group, its position rooted in decades of software development, enterprise relationships, and a steady expansion into new areas of computing. When observers scan the landscape of bluechip stocks, the company consistently ranks among the most prominent, a reflection of both its size and its central role in the modern digital economy. What distinguishes a bluechip from the broader universe of listed companies is durability. These businesses tend to generate consistent cash flows, maintain diversified revenue streams, and command the kind of balance-sheet strength that allows them to keep spending through periods of uncertainty. Microsoft embodies many of these traits, having built a franchise that spans consumer software, enterprise services, gaming, and cloud computing. That breadth is part of why the company is so frequently cited as a bellwether for the health of the technology sector as a whole. Microsoft operates across a remarkably wide set of markets. At its foundation sits the Windows operating system and the Office productivity suite, both of which remain deeply embedded in workplaces and homes around the world. Over time, the company has layered additional businesses on top of that base, most notably its cloud platform, which delivers computing power, storage, and a growing catalog of services to organizations of every size. This cloud franchise has become one of the central pillars of the modern enterprise, supporting everything from small startups to the largest multinational institutions. Beyond the cloud, the company maintains a substantial presence in gaming through its console and subscription offerings, in professional networking through its social platform for careers, and in developer tooling through its widely used code-hosting service. Each of these pieces contributes to a diversified whole, reducing reliance on any single product line. The result is a business that touches an enormous share of global computing activity, giving it a vantage point on trends that ripple across industries and geographies. Among the themes shaping the current market, few carry as much weight as the buildout of artificial intelligence infrastructure. Demand for the computing power needed to train and run advanced models has surged, and companies that supply that capacity have found themselves at the center of the conversation. Microsoft has positioned itself firmly within this movement, weaving AI capabilities across its cloud platform and its productivity applications while committing heavily to the data-center capacity required to meet growing demand. Recent earnings across the AI infrastructure landscape have been notably strong, reinforcing the sense that the underlying demand is real and durable rather than fleeting. For a company of Microsoft's scale, this dynamic matters a great deal, because its cloud business stands to benefit as organizations expand their use of AI-driven tools. The company has spoken frequently about embedding intelligent features throughout its product portfolio, and the market has kept a close eye on how that strategy translates into activity across its cloud and software divisions. The session unfolded within a market that has been navigating a delicate balance. On one hand, equities have marched to record levels, buoyed by resilient corporate earnings and enthusiasm around AI. On the other, climbing Treasury yields and an uncertain inflation trajectory have introduced a note of caution. Higher yields tend to weigh on the calculus around long-duration growth names, and technology companies frequently sit at the heart of that discussion. Microsoft, with its blend of steady cash generation and growth-oriented cloud franchise, occupies an interesting middle ground within that debate. Thin summer volumes added another layer to the picture. With many participants away from their desks and activity subdued, price moves can become exaggerated or, conversely, unusually muted. On this particular day, the mood leaned toward stillness, as the market seemed content to wait for the inflation data before making any decisive moves. That quietness extended across the large-capitalization technology group, where names like Microsoft traded in a composed and unhurried manner. Beyond technology, other corners of the market were generating their own headlines. Oil prices moved higher amid rising tensions involving the United States, Iran, and the strategically vital Strait of Hormuz, a waterway through which a significant share of global energy shipments passes. Energy names outperformed as a result, adding a rotational element to the session. While these developments sit somewhat apart from Microsoft's core business, they contribute to the overall tone of the market and influence how capital moves among sectors during periods of heightened geopolitical attention. The interplay between energy strength and technology steadiness illustrated the crosscurrents at work. Markets rarely move in a single direction all at once, and days like this one, where different sectors respond to different forces, highlight the layered nature of the current environment. For a diversified bluechip such as Microsoft, this kind of backdrop tends to reinforce its role as a stabilizing presence rather than a source of dramatic swings. The technology sector has been defined in recent times by the rapid ascent of artificial intelligence, the ongoing migration of workloads to the cloud, and the steady digitization of business processes across every industry. These trends have created substantial tailwinds for the largest software and infrastructure providers, Microsoft prominently among them. As organizations continue to modernize their operations, demand for cloud services, collaboration tools, and intelligent applications has remained robust. At the same time, the sector faces its share of complexity. Competition among the major cloud providers is intense, the capital required to build out data-center capacity is enormous, and questions about the pace and economics of AI adoption remain topics of active debate. Microsoft navigates these dynamics from a position of considerable strength, but the sector's evolution ensures that no participant can afford to stand still. The company's ability to keep pace with, and often help define, these trends is part of what keeps it central to conversations about the sector's direction. Microsoft's position within the technology landscape rests on the depth of its relationships with enterprises and the breadth of its product ecosystem. Organizations that adopt one part of its platform frequently find themselves drawing on others, creating a web of interconnected services that is difficult for competitors to replicate. This integration across productivity, cloud, and security offerings gives the company a durable foothold in the corporate world. The competitive landscape, however, is far from static. Rival cloud providers pursue the same customers, and the race to lead in artificial intelligence has drawn in a wide field of well-resourced participants. Microsoft competes by leaning on its established presence, its extensive partner network, and its willingness to commit aggressively to the infrastructure that underpins next-generation computing. The balance between defending its existing franchises and pushing into new frontiers defines much of the strategic story around the company. In recent periods, the company has directed considerable attention toward scaling its data-center footprint and integrating advanced AI features throughout its offerings. This operational focus reflects a broader industry recognition that the infrastructure supporting artificial intelligence will be a defining battleground for years to come. Microsoft has signaled its intention to remain at the forefront of that effort, channeling resources into the physical and computational capacity that intelligent applications require. This emphasis on infrastructure carries meaningful implications for how the business operates. Building and maintaining data centers is a capital-intensive undertaking, and the scale of the commitment reflects confidence in the durability of demand. As the AI infrastructure narrative continued to draw favorable earnings commentary across the sector, Microsoft's own positioning within that story remained a focal point for market participants weighing the health of the technology complex. No company of Microsoft's size operates without confronting significant challenges. The regulatory environment surrounding large technology firms has grown more attentive, with authorities in multiple jurisdictions scrutinizing questions of competition, data handling, and market power. Navigating this landscape requires ongoing engagement and adaptation. The capital intensity of the AI buildout also introduces its own pressures, as the enormous sums directed toward infrastructure must eventually be matched by durable demand. Currency movements, shifting enterprise spending patterns, and the broader macroeconomic climate all add further layers of complexity. A company that generates revenue across the globe is naturally sensitive to changes in economic conditions in different regions. These challenges do not diminish Microsoft's standing, but they underscore that even the most established bluechip names operate within an environment of constant change and must continually adapt to preserve their positions. Microsoft's importance to the wider market extends well beyond its own share performance. As one of the largest components of major indices, its movements carry weight for the broad tape, and shifts in sentiment toward the company often echo across the technology sector and beyond. When observers gauge the health of large-capitalization equities, Microsoft frequently serves as a reference point, a role that reflects both its scale and its central position in the digital economy. For anyone tracking bluechip stocks, the company remains a recurring name in conversations about the market's direction. On a day defined by anticipation ahead of the inflation data, that relevance was on full display. The company's steady demeanor mirrored the broader market's composure, and its ongoing role in the AI infrastructure story kept it woven into the day's dominant themes. As the market awaited the July CPI print, Microsoft stood as a familiar anchor within a landscape marked by caution, crosscurrents, and the ever-present pull of technological change. The session ultimately reinforced a pattern that has held for some time: in moments of uncertainty, the market tends to gravitate toward the largest and most established names as it recalibrates. Microsoft, with its diversified operations and its deep involvement in the defining technology trends of the era, once again found itself at the center of that gravitational pull, a quiet but persistent presence as the market waited for its next signal. The migration of computing workloads from on-premises servers to the cloud represents one of the most consequential shifts of the modern technology era, and Microsoft has been a central beneficiary of that transition. Organizations that once maintained sprawling in-house data centers have increasingly turned to cloud providers for flexibility, scale, and access to advanced capabilities they could not easily build on their own. This structural change has given the company a growing base of recurring activity that spans industries as varied as finance, healthcare, manufacturing, and government. What makes the cloud so pivotal is the way it compounds over time. As organizations deepen their reliance on cloud platforms, they tend to adopt additional services, integrate more of their operations, and build applications that assume the availability of elastic computing power. Microsoft has worked to make its platform the natural home for these expanding needs, layering artificial intelligence, data analytics, and security offerings on top of its core infrastructure. The cumulative effect is a franchise that grows more embedded with each passing year, reinforcing the company's standing among the most durable names in the technology landscape. Periods of market uncertainty often reveal the distinctive character of bluechip names. When participants grow cautious, capital frequently gravitates toward businesses perceived as stable and enduring, and the largest technology franchises tend to feature prominently in that flight to familiarity. Microsoft's blend of steady cash generation and exposure to fast-growing areas of computing gives it a dual appeal, allowing it to serve as both a defensive anchor and a participant in the market's growth themes. That combination helps explain why the company remains so frequently discussed whenever the broad tape enters a wait-and-see phase. The session ahead of the inflation data offered a textbook illustration of this behavior. With the market reluctant to commit to a direction, the largest and most established names traded in a measured fashion, absorbing the day's crosscurrents without dramatic swings. Microsoft's composure amid the quiet reflected the broader tendency of bluechip stocks to provide a sense of ballast during uncertain stretches, a quality that has long been part of their appeal to a wide range of market participants navigating shifting conditions. title: Up 26% Since July 29, Is It Too Late to Buy Microsoft Stock? - The Globe and Mail
content: Microsoft stock looked cheap ahead of its latest earnings report. The tech giant reassured investors by keeping its capital expenditure guidance steady. Microsoft(NASDAQ: MSFT) stock has been on quite a run since the company reported its results for the fourth quarter of its fiscal 2026 (which ended June 30). Microsoft delivered those results after the close of trading on July 29, and investors sent the stock skyrocketing the following day. They have continued bidding the stock higher, and it's now up by an impressive 26% since the report came out. That's a huge run in a short time frame, and for a company as large as Microsoft, it may make investors feel like they've missed the boat. So, is it too late to buy shares for now? Or is this rally an indication of something new? Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again.In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Microsoft is a major software company that is also diving deep into AI. It is exposed to AI in two ways: its internal products and its cloud computing business. Microsoft Copilot is its in-house AI tool meant to provide general AI use and also interface with the Office suite of productivity titles. This product reached over 30 million paid seats in the quarter, showcasing strong growth. However, cloud computing is more of a focus area for investors. Microsoft Azure continued to grow rapidly, with revenue rising 43% year over year. To make money, though, it must build cloud computing capacity and infrastructure, which is why Microsoft is spending hundreds of billions of dollars on data centers. While some of Microsoft's hyperscaler competitors, like Amazon(NASDAQ: AMZN) and Alphabet(NASDAQ: GOOG)(NASDAQ: GOOGL), recently increased their already lofty spending capex expectations for 2026, Microsoft left its capex guidance unchanged. The market is worried that the AI hyperscalers may be overspending on their data center build-outs, so the news that Microsoft was not planning to further accelerate its outlays this year likely helped bolster its share price. Still, the biggest reason why Microsoft had such a rapid rise following its earnings report was how cheap the stock was ahead of it. At the start of July and leading up to the release date, Microsoft stock traded for less than 20 times forward earnings -- its cheapest valuation in a long time. Considering how strong a business Microsoft is, this valuation level made no sense. Microsoft now trades at a far more reasonable level. It's still on the low end of its recent levels, but it is also at the higher end of the valuation spectrum compared to some of its big tech peers. In short, many investors have missed their opportunity to buy Microsoft at the dirt cheap levels it traded at earlier this summer. While I still think Microsoft can be a successful and market-beating investment over the next few years, a lot of the growth the stock had coming was delivered in just a few days. title: Is Microsoft Stock Still The Asset-Light Business You Bought? - Trefis
content:
Its capital spending has multiplied as a share of revenue while its free-cash-flow margin has thinned, which changes what a holder is underwriting. Microsoft (MSFT)‘s product list still reads like a software company’s; its spending no longer does. Capital spending now takes more than three times its historical share of revenue, and the free-cash-flow margin has thinned. For a holder the question is not whether the business is good, but whether this is still the business you bought. In the trailing data through the June 2026 quarter, capital spending runs at 34.9% of revenue against a 10.6% history, and the full-year free-cash-flow margin has dropped to 20.2% from a 29.6% historical average. Zooming in on the most recent quarter, operating cash flow rose 30% year over year in fiscal Q4 2026, while Q4 free cash flow stood at $19.6 billion—a figure management ties directly to the higher capital spending. The cash engine has not weakened; less of what it produces reaches you. Microsoft booked more than $331 billion of revenue in fiscal 2026, the base that capital-spending share comes out of. The company added 31 new data centers in fiscal Q4 2026, taking the year’s total to 88, and in that quarter roughly two-thirds of its capital expenditure went into short-lived assets, primarily CPUs and GPUs, with the remainder in long-lived assets. A business that spent a tenth of revenue on capacity and one that spends a third of it, mostly on equipment that has to be replaced, are not the same asset to own. What you are being asked to judge now is whether the capital going in comes back out. The reading does not show a lender problem: debt is 7.5% of total assets against a 19.0% history. Balance-sheet strength of that kind is one of the things the Trefis High Quality Portfolio insists on in its holdings. Nor is the spending about to step back down: management expects fiscal 2027 capital expenditures to grow year over year. On the company’s own fourteen-year record, these three readings have never sat this far from their own norms at the same time. Re-underwriting is not the same as selling. Demand for Azure exceeded available capacity in fiscal Q4 2026, and management has guided Azure revenue growth of approximately 45% in constant currency for fiscal Q1 2027, which is what the spending is meant to buy. The stock has returned -2.7% over the past twelve months, 23.7 points behind the market, and sits about 6.5% below its 52-week high, lagging the market without falling far from its own high. Reading the return on that spending is getting harder: from fiscal 2027 Microsoft has stretched the assumed useful life of its data centers and office buildings from 15 to 25 years, and more future data-center leases move from finance leases into operating leases, which sit outside the capital expenditure line. So judge the build on free-cash-flow margin rather than on capex alone, because from fiscal 2027 the lease payments moving off the capital expenditure line still run through cash flow. Apply that test to any company whose guidance keeps climbing while its capital bill does too. Re-underwriting a company mid-build is real work, and it has to be redone for every name you hold. The Trefis High Quality Portfolio does that job by rule rather than by conviction, applied across a basket instead of one name. That portfolio has a track record of outpacing the three major indices – the S&P 500, S&P Mid-cap, and Russell 2000. title: I've Been Wrong About Microsoft Stock for Years. Here's Why I'm Finally Changing My Mind. - The Motley Fool
content: Microsoft has gone from looking overpriced to a compelling long-term buy as its AI and cloud businesses continue to drive strong growth, at a valuation that no longer seems excessive. For the last five years, I've been the person rolling my eyes at Microsoft's (MSFT -2.26%) valuation and calling it priced for perfection. Today, after its latest set of numbers and the way the company has embedded itself into AI, cloud, and everyday work, I'm finally willing to say it: At these levels, Microsoft is an easy buy for a long‑term investor. Back in the 2021 to 2022 time frame, my skepticism sounded reasonable. Microsoft was trading at a rich multiple compared with its own history, and it felt like everyone already knew the bull case: dominant Windows, sticky Office, and fast‑growing Azure. I kept waiting for growth to slow or margins to crack. Instead, 2026 gave a very different picture. In the fiscal year that ended June 30, Microsoft's revenue climbed 18% to more than $331 billion, while operating income rose 21% to more than $155 billion. Net income hit $133.7 billion, with full‑year EPS growth comfortably above 20% even after stripping out gains from OpenAI and Anthropic investments. Those are not the numbers of a mature company just coasting on its legacy. The AI story is where I was most wrong. I assumed the AI halo would be mostly narrative. Instead, it has become a concrete, growing business. In the latest quarter, revenue reached $90 billion, up 18% year over year, driven by 32% growth in the Intelligent Cloud segment and Azure revenue now surpassing $100 billion annually. Microsoft says its AI business has crossed a $37 billion annual run rate, growing 123% year over year. This is not really a side hustle. It's a growth engine. On top of this, Azure grew 43% year over year in fiscal Q4 2026, and  CEO Satya Nadella said Microsoft's custom AI chips can deliver up to 40% better performance per watt, potentially improving cloud margins and earnings. Copilot is the clearest proof that this is real monetization, not just GPU reselling. Microsoft 365 Copilot has already passed 30 million paid seats, with net seat adds more than doubling quarter over quarter as enterprises move from pilots to production. Microsoft is rolling Copilot out across knowledge work, coding, security, and even as a super app that ties consumer and commercial experiences together. That means AI is getting woven into the subscription backbone of the company's productivity and business software. The part that finally changed my mind, though, is the valuation-versus-execution debate. As of early August 2026, Microsoft trades at a trailing P/E of 28 to 28.5, which is slightly below its 10‑year average of 30.  Forward P/E estimates sit around 25 based on current consensus, even as the company continues to grow revenue in the high teens and EPS in the low-to-mid‑20s. That is not cheap in an absolute sense, but for a business with Microsoft's moat and growth profile, it looks more like fair for a wonderful company than irrational exuberance. Could I wait for a better entry point? Sure. There will always be a pullback. But the last five years have taught me that trying to shave a few multiple points off the price has been far more costly than simply owning a compounding machine that keeps finding new profit pools -- first cloud, now AI, and next whatever sits on top of that stack. Microsoft today is not just a safe blue chip; it is one of the few companies genuinely defining the next era of enterprise computing. I spent half a decade treating it as too expensive. Now I'm much more worried about the opportunity cost of staying on the sidelines. Micah Zimmerman has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. title: Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Leads Peers On Fundamentals But Trails Badly On Stock Returns - foreignpolicyjournal.com
content: By David Prior | Aug 12, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), trading at approximately $506.06 per share, is the dominant engine behind the corporate AI push, yet its stock has significantly underperformed its closest rivals over the past year. The company’s operating margin of 47% is the highest among its competitive peer group, which includes Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Oracle, and Salesforce. Revenue grew 17.8% over the last twelve months, a figure second only to Alphabet’s 20% growth rate within that same peer set. Despite those elite fundamentals, Microsoft’s twelve-month stock return stands at -2.1%, a stark contrast to Alphabet’s +82% and Apple’s +41% over the same period. The valuation picture adds another layer of complexity, with Microsoft trading at 28.1 times earnings compared to Alphabet’s far cheaper multiple of 17.8. That premium is not being paid for past performance but for a projected AI-powered future, with Azure and other cloud services revenue growing 43% in the latest reported period. Management highlighted that the company now has “over 30 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats,” with seat additions rapidly increasing as enterprise adoption of AI tools accelerates. The capital cost of building out that AI infrastructure is substantial, with capital expenditures reaching $41 billion in the last reported quarter alone, raising investor questions about potential overcapacity if demand falters. Legacy segments are creating a meaningful drag on overall performance, with Xbox revenue declining 10% in the latest quarter and management projecting that Windows OEM and Devices revenue will “decline in the high teens” in the upcoming fiscal year. The central tension for investors is whether the explosive growth in AI-centric businesses can outpace the steady erosion in older product lines and justify the current premium valuation. title: Michael Burry Exits MSFT, Closes ORCL Short Position – Why He Changed His Tech Trades? - Stocktwits
content: “Big Short” investor Michael Burry on Tuesday said he sold off Microsoft shares, closed his short position in Oracle stock, and partially reduced his bearish bet in Palantir stock. Burry’s trades come just as Big Tech delivered a robust set of quarterly earnings.    Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet beat revenue and profit expectations, while the latter two also raised their capital expenditure forecasts for the year. Palantir, too, reported blowout results, which sent its stock up nearly 30% on Tuesday. Oracle has yet to announce the date for its quarterly results. Burry first disclosed a position in Microsoft in April and recently unwound it, according to a trading update on his Substack page. “That position benefitted from some lucky timing, and I cannot say my enthusiasm for Microsoft’s earnings report rose to the same level as that of the market,” Burry wrote. The Windows-maker issued a remarkably strong quarterly report last week. Revenue increased 19% in the company’s fiscal fourth quarter, with Azure Cloud and other services’ sales climbing 43% – both were above Wall Street’s projections at the time. The stock has soared over 25% in the four sessions since Microsoft issued the results. On the Oracle trade, Burry said, “These were the January 2027 low 100s strikes, and I decided not to roll them. The profit there was substantial, and so I left it at that. Should volatility come down, I may re-enter Oracle puts.” ORCL stock declined 11% in July, and got a lift this month. Burry has been one of the most vocal critics of Palantir, routinely flagging concerns with the company’s accounting and spending. He sold or let expire his January put options on PLTR, but kept his direct short position in stock. Palantir’s second-quarter sales nearly doubled to $1.94 billion, with U.S. commercial sales surging 149% and U.S. government sales rising 90%, according to results issued on Monday. The top and bottom lines comfortably beat expectations of $1.81 billion in revenue and EPS of $0.35. The company also raised its 2026 revenue forecast to a range of $8.15 billion to $8.16 billion, up from a prior top-end range of around $7.66 billion. Of the three stocks, Palantir is the most richly valued, trading at 86.2 times its forward earnings. Microsoft trades at 25 times and Oracle at 18.1 times. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment was ‘neutral’ for ORCL, and ‘extremely bullish’ for PLTR and MSFT. Some traders asserted that PLTR and MSFT were poised to cool off in the coming days. Yum! Brands voluntarily removed shredded lettuce from Taco Bell restaurants across the U.S. in July after concerns surrounding ingredients supplied by Taylor Farms. The CDC and FDA linked a Taco Bell lettuce outbreak to a parasite infection called cyclosporiasis, which sickened nearly 2,000 people in nine states and sent almost 100 people to hospitals. The outbreak hurt YUM stock at first, while other restaurant companies also saw declines as investors worried about possible lettuce supply problems. The FDA is also reviewing multiple possible ingredients. Sandisk and Kioxia unveiled their 10th-gen quad-level-cell (QLC) 3D flash tech at the Future of Memory and Storage (FMS) Conference on Tuesday. The 332-layer design delivers up to 60% greater bit density than the company’s eighth-gen tech and exceeds 37 gigabits per square millimeter, which they called an industry high. It is also the first QLC 3D flash tech to achieve a 4.8-gigabit-per-second interface. The tech manufactures the memory array and its control circuitry on separate wafers before bonding them together, improving density, bandwidth and production efficiency. These gains target the growing storage, power and cooling demands created by AI training, inference and hyperscale data centers. The QLC tech is a Sandisk-Kioxia project, but it complements Sandisk’s work with SK Hynix on high-bandwidth flash (HBF). Sandisk and SK Hynix on Tuesday released the first HBF technical specification through the Open Compute Project, with Google and Tenstorrent contributing to its development. The specification gives chip and system designers a common framework for placing larger amounts of flash memory closer to AI processors. HBF will supplement traditional high-bandwidth memory by providing greater near-compute capacity for AI inference, potentially improving model-serving performance, power consumption and costs. Shares of Sandisk (SNDK) and SK Hynix (SKHY) rose in early morning trade on Tuesday after the companies unveiled the first industry standard for High Bandwidth Flash (HBF), a new memory technology that could make it easier for AI systems built around different chipmakers to work together. SNDK stock rose as much as 2.3% in pre-market trade, while SKHY stock gained just under 2%. Retail sentiment around SNDK remained in ‘extremely bullish’ territory over the past day, while sentiment around SKHY fell to ‘neutral’ from ‘bullish’ territory over the past day. Chatter for both remained at ‘extremely high’ levels. The HBF specification, released through the Open Compute Project (OCP), is not a commercial product but an open blueprint for the next generation of AI memory. Developed by Sandisk and SK Hynix with contributions from Alphabet's (GOOG, GOOGL) Google and AI chip startup Tenstorrent, HBF is designed to bridge the gap between ultra-fast but capacity-constrained High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) and slower, high-capacity SSDs by using NAND flash optimized for much higher data transfer speeds. One of the biggest changes is that HBF adopts the Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) standard, allowing the technology to connect with processors from multiple vendors instead of relying on proprietary interconnects. In practice, that means future AI servers could combine Nvidia (NVDA) GPUs with processors from Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Intel (INTC), or custom AI accelerators while using the same memory architecture. An open HBF standard could gradually reduce that dependence by giving hyperscalers and enterprise customers a common memory layer that works across multiple chip architectures. The shift comes as companies, including Google, Amazon (AMZN), Microsoft (MSFT), and Meta (META), invest billions of dollars in developing their own AI accelerators to reduce their reliance on Nvidia. At the same time, newer players and memory manufacturers, including China's CXMT, are racing to catch up in technologies such as HBM and advanced chip packaging. SK Hynix also received a slew of bullish calls from Wall Street on Tuesday morning. RBC Capital’s Srini Pajjuri initiated coverage with an ‘Outperform’ rating and a $200 price target. Stifel gave SKHY stock a ‘Buy’ rating and $240 price target, calling DRAM “a vital component of AI hardware infrastructure” and stating that SK Hynix’s execution remains undervalued. William Blair also initiated at ‘Outperform’, noting that tight near‑term supply has tripled AI memory prices and pushed SK Hynix to record revenues and margins, with free cash flow projected to more than double by 2028. title: Microsoft Stock Runs One Of The Market’s Biggest Cash-Return Machines - Trefis
content:
Microsoft showered investors with one of the largest cash returns on the market, but the real story is what that spending says about the tech giant’s future. Over the last five years, Microsoft (MSFT) handed its owners $223 billion in cash, a figure so large it ranks as the 3rd highest among all U.S. companies. While that sum dwarfs the $5.8 billion returned by the median S&P 500 firm in absolute dollars, it equals just 6.0% of Microsoft’s entire market value—well below the 16.2% proportion returned by the median firm. For an owner of the stock, which trades around $499.99 a share after underperforming the market over the last year, this torrent of cash raises a sharp question: With a total return that trailed the index over that five-year period, was this large payout a sign of extraordinary financial strength or a consolation prize for a business in a complex transition? The $223 billion machine is funded by one of the most profitable enterprises on the planet. The cash, split between $113 billion in share repurchases and $110 billion in dividends, flows directly from a business firing on its most important cylinder. The company’s annual revenue recently surpassed $331 billion, and its broader Microsoft Cloud business alone is a behemoth with revenue over $214 billion. In its latest quarter, revenue from Azure and other cloud services grew 43%, a rapid pace for a business of its scale. Demand for its AI infrastructure is so intense that management stated, “Customer demand continues to exceed available capacity.” This is the source of the cash, a high-margin, high-growth cloud operation that generates more money than the company currently needs to run its day-to-day operations. Despite the gusher of cash, holding the stock was not a market-beating experience. Over the five-year payout period, Microsoft stock delivered a total return of +83%, a strong result that nonetheless trailed the S&P 500’s +88% return. Rather than a sign of underinvestment, the gap highlights a business in two distinct cycles: a booming cloud segment funding the payout, and legacy divisions navigating shifting demand and strategic overhauls. While the AI-fueled cloud business booms, legacy segments are contracting. Management expects revenue from its Windows OEM and Devices segment to “decline in the high teens for the fiscal year.” Its Xbox division saw revenue decrease 10% in the last quarter. This is the honest catch for investors. The enormous capital return coincides with a strategic pivot where growth is becoming highly concentrated in AI and the cloud, while older, foundational businesses are fading. The tension between Microsoft’s soaring Azure costs and its profit margins is a key part of this story. The capital-return story is not about a company out of ideas, but one making a large, focused bet on an AI-centric future while managing the slow decline of other divisions. For those holding Microsoft, the question is whether the new growth engine can carry the weight of the whole company. The single most important metric to watch is how this transition affects profitability. Management has been clear about the scale of investment required. The test of their discipline will be in the bottom line. They have guided that for the full fiscal year, operating margins “should be down less than 1 point.” Holding that line would be the clearest signal that the AI bet is profitable enough to power the entire Microsoft machine for years to come, in addition to driving revenue. title: Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Positioned To Rival OpenAI And Anthropic With $100B-Per-GW Inference Revenue Opportunity, SemiAnalysis Reports - foreignpolicyjournal.com
content: By David Prior | Aug 10, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) could emerge as a dominant force in AI inference, matching frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic in revenue potential, according to semiconductor research firm SemiAnalysis. The firm’s proprietary models estimate that frontier AI companies can generate more than $100 billion in annual revenue per gigawatt of compute capacity, underscoring the fierce race to secure data-center power. AI inference refers to the process of running a trained AI model in the cloud to generate real-time responses, predictions, or outputs for end users. SemiAnalysis argues that Microsoft is uniquely positioned to capture these economics, citing the company’s access to OpenAI models without bearing the burden of training costs. “Having full access to OpenAI models, they can generate the same revenue and margin per MW, while paying none of the training costs,” SemiAnalysis wrote in its analysis. The April 2026 renegotiation of Microsoft’s deal with OpenAI proved pivotal, removing the old 20% revenue share arrangement that had previously weighed on Microsoft’s returns. “Satya [Nadella] nailed the negotiations with OpenAI: the deal reworked in April 2026 dropped the old 20% revenue share from the equation. Put simply, Microsoft has a giant incentive to procure as many MWs as possible, as fast as possible.” Microsoft Azure’s revenue is currently growing at approximately 42% year over year, but SemiAnalysis suggests that figure could exceed 100% growth by next year as more capacity comes online and is directed toward inference workloads. Microsoft has already signed 10 gigawatts of data-center contracts year-to-date, representing over $300 billion in total contract value, with SemiAnalysis expecting additional agreements to be announced for capacity coming online over the next two years. SpaceX is emerging as a surprising but formidable competitor in the compute market, with CEO Elon Musk stating during the company’s first-ever earnings report that SpaceX “conservatively” expects to build and deliver an additional 6 to 8 gigawatts of capacity next year, with potential to exceed 10 gigawatts. SemiAnalysis noted that its analysis of potential sites, power equipment, and construction timelines suggests SpaceX’s target is achievable, pointing to the company’s ability to build at remarkable speed. The company constructed the 300-megawatt Colossus 1 facility in just 122 days, while its Southaven power plant expanded from 495 megawatts in February to 1.7 gigawatts by July, according to the report. SemiAnalysis estimates SpaceX could reach approximately $300 billion in annual recurring revenue even if only half of its incremental 2027 capacity is monetized, with the remainder consumed by xAI and Cursor for model training. On retail sentiment platform Stocktwits, sentiment was rated “neutral” for MSFT and “bullish” for SpaceX as of Monday, reflecting divergent investor enthusiasm between the two compute heavyweights. MSFT stock has gained over 28% since its earnings report on July 20, while SPCX has climbed 15.5% since SpaceX’s earnings report on August 12, reflecting growing investor confidence in the AI infrastructure buildout.
